QnA 1 · What does MO→MAP change for fused attention?

One mo.custom becomes one map.iter.opaque containing a map.call.opaque. The surrounding mo.graph still has three tensor arguments and one tensor result. The new nested region makes the implementation's inputs and output destination explicit. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:159 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:179 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:238

BEFORE · IR1 graph body
  %o = mo.custom(%q, %k, %v)
       symbol="modular_ops::fused_attention_custom"
       parameters={BD=8, BN=16}, device=gpu:0
  mo.output %o

AFTER · source-derived schematic, same external contract
  %o_map = map.iter.opaque
      inputs  (%q as %qi:T0, %k as %ki:T0, %v as %vi:T0)
      outputs (%oi:T0) {
    map.call.opaque @PKG.fused_attention.FusedAttention
      parameters={BD=8, BN=16}
      inputs(%qi, %ki, %vi) outputs(%oi)
      kernelName="modular_ops::fused_attention_custom"
  } device=gpu:0, dispatch=deferred
  mo.output %o_map

T0 = float32[32,32] on gpu:0
PKG = illustrative name for the imported P1 package

The actual fully qualified symbol comes from the imported declaration; PKG above is a readable stand-in. The pass rewires users to the new results and erases the old operation in IR1. This is replacement of native IR objects, not changing a Python TensorValue into a MAP wrapper. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:241 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:255 ↗ FrameworkFrontend.cpp:377

This kernel is an ordinary execute registration, not an elementwise or reduction registration. It therefore follows lowerToOpaque, rather than the branches that create a scalar elementwise loop or a row reduction body. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:74 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:717 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:724 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:756

SOURCE · scheduling and ownership. buildStage adds pass objects; runGCPipeline later calls pm.run(moduleOp). The worklist holds pointers into the compiler's IR1 module. The newly created iterator owns its region and block; that block owns its arguments and nested operations. The temporary registry/adaptor/mapping objects help select and describe a declaration. The new call retains a symbol reference and attributes in IR1. Pipeline execution ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:768 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:180 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:238

Decision Matched path Skipped or rejected path
Stable-tensor marking before MO→MAP A device graph, a registered build_graph entry, and a stable-tensor role cause mo.stable.create to be inserted on that operand. An ordinary graph, missing build_graph, or ordinary tensor role needs no marker. This does not add a fourth attention input.
Registered implementation Imported declaration determines the elementwise/reduction/opaque branch. An adaptor lookup error returns a successful null result from lowerOp; this pass leaves the MO op in place.
Fused I/O role A tensor role marked fusible gets a load/store closure. An ordinary tensor passes directly; an unsupported fused non-tensor role emits an error.
Dispatch stampAsyncLaunch records immediate for operations selected by kernelRequiresSyncLaunch, including transpose. Other operations, including this custom call, receive deferred; no operation executes while this field is set.

The marking guards and mutation are in MarkStableTensorsPass::runOnOperation and StableCreateOp construction. The other branches are in lowerOp, lowerToOpaque, and the dispatch helper. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:705 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:205 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:219 ↗ MOUtils.cpp:27

The FailureOr<Operation *> return deserves care: a null successful value also follows successful elementwise/view/reduction replacement. The pass tests failed(...), not whether the pointer is null. An opaque replacement returns the new iterator pointer. Thus a null result alone cannot tell a caller whether an operation changed. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:714 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:721 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:728 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:761 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:257 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:788

QnA 3 · Why are there now four body arguments? Did G1 gain an input?

The four arguments belong to a new nested MAP body. Three shadow inputs; the fourth denotes where this implementation writes the output. The outer graph's caller still supplies only Q, K and V. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:179 ↗ fused_attention.py:61

IR1 : builtin.module
└─ mo.graph @fused_attention
   └─ graph body block                  ← still THREE user inputs
      ├─ %q : T0
      ├─ %k : T0
      ├─ %v : T0
      └─ %o_map = map.iter.opaque
         └─ body region → ONE block     ← FOUR local arguments
            ├─ %qi : T0  ← Q input
            ├─ %ki : T0  ← K input
            ├─ %vi : T0  ← V input
            ├─ %oi : T0  ← output destination
            └─ map.call.opaque inputs(%qi,%ki,%vi) outputs(%oi)

Outer result %o_map and inner output destination %oi have different roles.
No fourth user tensor is added to G1.inputs.

This is destination-passing style: the implementation writes a supplied output destination. In this pass it is an IR argument; actual output storage is introduced by later runtime lowering. The nested call does not return a new tensor-valued SSA result for this case. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:238 ↗ MOGGOps.cpp:788

A !mo.opaque by-value result has a different branch: it has no destination block argument and uses map.yield. That branch does not apply to the tensor result here. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:189 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:251

QnA 5 · When does MAP expose scalar loads and stores? Give an example.

For an elementwise registered operation, the other MOToMAP branch exposes scalar computation indexed over the tensor. The original attention registration does not use that branch. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:260 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:724

ILLUSTRATIVE elementwise operation, separate from attention
BEFORE: %c = mo.add(%a,%b) : float32[2,3]

AFTER: map.iter.elementwise over [2,3]
       └─ body argument %idx : !map.index<2>
          ├─ %av = map.load A[%idx]
          ├─ %bv = map.load B[%idx]
          ├─ %cv = registered scalar Add(%av,%bv)
          └─ map.store C[%idx] = %cv

At index [1,2]: A[1,2]=4, B[1,2]=5 → C[1,2]=9.
The loop describes work; creating the IR does not run those loads.

The implementation explicitly creates one load per tensor input, a scalar registered call and a store. These bodies give later fusion passes something they can safely combine. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:260

For an opaque implementation, the declaration can instead request FusedInputTensor or FusedOutputTensor. MOToMAP then inserts load prologues or store epilogues. Their callbacks let compatible neighboring computations participate in fusion. The ordinary InputTensor/OutputTensor roles in this attention example select the direct-argument paths. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:210 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:224 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:82

TEST · inspected expectation: the repository's plain-output test expects map.call.opaque to write the raw output argument and explicitly rejects an epilogue. Its fused-output comparison expects a map.iter.epilogue. ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:41 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:20

QnA 6 · What does the next stage receive?

MAP optimization input, attention path
├─ one map.iter.opaque
│  ├─ inputs: Q, K, V
│  ├─ output destination: O
│  ├─ call: P1's FusedAttention declaration
│  └─ params: BN=16, BD=8
└─ outer mo.output consumes the iterator result

No scalar QK/softmax/PV body has been exposed to MAP.
No data pointers or GPU allocations exist merely from constructing these ops.

The enclosing module may contain several dialects at this boundary: mo.graph and its tensor types coexist with MAP operations and MOGG declaration metadata. MO→MAP is a transformation of selected operations, not a requirement that every mo.* object disappear at once. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:780 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:41 ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:585

QnA 7 · How does MO→MAP rewrite concrete attention, fused-tensor, elementwise, view, reduction and mutable-store operations? For each example, show the input values and shapes, before/after IR, changed operands and blocks, native implementation, and the test or guard that establishes the result.

SOURCE / TEST · nine worked examples. The IR below is schematic: declarations, type repetitions and generated symbol prefixes are shortened. Native C++ excerpts retain their implementation statements. Numerical values are illustrative contract checks; the compiler constructs these operations without evaluating these arrays. The cited .mlir files supply independent test graphs to mo-opt. Their RUN commands identify the passes under test, and CHECK comments describe expected printed IR; none of these tests was executed for this reader.

Example 1 · How do three attention inputs become four local block arguments without changing the graph signature?

SOURCE · actual attention route. The accelerator configuration supplies Q, K and V with shape [32,32], float32, and parameters BD=8, BN=16. Its registered execute signature requests three ordinary InputTensor values and one ordinary OutputTensor. That signature determines the absence of prologue/epilogue closures. ↗ fused_attention.py:35 ↗ fused_attention.py:57 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:74 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:82

BEFORE · IR1, schematic
  graph inputs %q, %k, %v : f32[32,32] on gpu:0   // three caller-supplied tensors
  %o = mo.custom(%q,%k,%v)                       // one tensor-valued operation
       symbol="modular_ops::fused_attention_custom"
       parameters={BD=8, BN=16}, device=gpu:0
  mo.output %o                                  // one externally visible result

AFTER · same graph signature
  %r = map.iter.opaque inputs(%q,%k,%v)           // replacement op owns a region
       outputs(%oi : f32[32,32]) {               // one local output destination
    ^body(%qi,%ki,%vi,%oi):                      // all four are new block arguments
      map.call.opaque @PKG.FusedAttention         // selected declaration, same function
        [BD=8, BN=16] inputs(%qi,%ki,%vi)
        outputs(%oi)                            // writes into the local destination
  } device=gpu:0, dispatch=deferred
  mo.output %r                                  // old %o use rewired to %r

lowerToOpaque first creates the enclosing result-bearing operation, then its body block. This excerpt explains why an output destination is a block argument while the outer output is an SSA result:

Block *body = builder.createBlock(&opaque.getBody());
SmallVector<BlockArgument> ins;
for (Value operand : nonChainOperands)
  ins.push_back(body->addArgument(operand.getType(), loc));

The following result-type loop appends ordinary output arguments; it skips chains and by-value !mo.opaque results. For attention it appends exactly one tensor argument, %oi. The input mapping selects %qi/%ki/%vi directly, and the output mapping selects %oi directly. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:179 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:186 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:201 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:215

The final mutation is small but essential:

op->replaceAllUsesWith(opaque.getResults());
op->erase();

This redirects mo.output and any other user before deleting the old native operation. It preserves the result type while changing the producer object. The original Python graph G1 remains outside this IR1 rewrite. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:255 ↗ FrameworkFrontend.cpp:377

Object Before After
Outer graph arguments %q,%k,%v Same three arguments
Computation result %o from mo.custom %r from map.iter.opaque
Nested body None on this custom op One region, one block, four arguments
Nested call result Not applicable No tensor SSA return; %oi is a destination
Parameters BD=8, BN=16 attributes Same normalized integer attributes

For an illustrative arithmetic check, take every Q entry as zero, finite K entries, and V[j,d]=j for j=0…31. The unscaled attention contract gives equal weights 1/32, so every output feature is (0+…+31)/32 = 15.5. Both IR forms name the same implementation and input tensors; this stage neither evaluates the average nor expands softmax. The authored attention arithmetic remains in the registered implementation. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:90 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:99 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:238

Guard and comparison. A registered elementwise custom kernel would take the earlier elementwise branch even though its MO operation is also named mo.custom. Conversely, no imported declaration means getMojoKernelAdaptor fails and lowerOp leaves the op untouched at this stage. TEST: opaque-kernels.mlir line 1 imports signature-only kernels and runs --mo-to-map; its @one_plain expectation forbids an epilogue. Line 2 omits the import, and the DISABLED checks require surviving mo.custom. Those tests validate the generic ordinary-output route and registry dependence; they do not run this attention kernel. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:708 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:725 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:1 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:2 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:37 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:95

Example 2 · Why does a fused output gain a store callback while an ordinary output remains a direct argument?

TEST · output-role comparison. The supplied test input @two_partial is a custom operation with one [2,2] f32 input and two [2,2] f32 results. The selected signature marks only the first output as fused. Its RUN imports %kernel_api_test_lib before --mo-to-map; CHECK requires one epilogue, CHECK-NOT excludes a second, and the call receives (epilogue, raw-output) in result order. These are signature-only kernels, so the test establishes structure rather than a particular numerical function. ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:1 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:76 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:80 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:87

BEFORE · schematic test operation
  %u,%v = mo.custom @map_lower_partial_fused_outputs(%a) // two tensor results
  mo.output %u,%v                                      // expose both results

AFTER · both result destinations remain explicit
  %r0,%r1 = map.iter.opaque inputs(%a as %ai)           // one input block argument
    outputs(%o0:f32[2,2], %o1:f32[2,2]) {              // two destination arguments
    %e0 = map.iter.epilogue(%value:f32, %i:index<2>)    // receives one produced scalar
      capturing(%cap=%o0) {                           // local reference to output 0
        map.store %cap[%i] = %value                   // identity store callback
      }
    map.call.opaque @MapLowerPartialFusedOutputs      // same registered implementation
      inputs(%ai) outputs(%e0,%o1)                    // fused first, ordinary second
  }
  mo.output %r0,%r1                                  // same external two-result contract

The native decision reads the declaration mapping, not the operation name or tensor size:

for (const auto &[idx, arg] : mapping.resultMapping)
  outputFusible[idx] = arg.isFusedTensorType();

The output loop passes an ordinary output straight through. For a fusible tensor output it instead pushes buildStoreEpilogue(...).getResult() into callOutputs. The epilogue builder creates block arguments in the order scalar value, index, captured destination, then inserts the store. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:141 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:215 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:224 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:75

BlockArgument val = body->addArgument(outType.getElementType(), loc);
BlockArgument idx = body->addArgument(indexType, loc);
BlockArgument cap = body->addArgument(out.getType(), loc);
builder.setInsertionPointToStart(body);
MAP::StoreOp::create(builder, loc, /*tensor=*/cap, /*index=*/idx,
                     /*value=*/val);

For a concrete callback invocation, if the implementation supplies value=7 at index [1,0], the new closure records O0[1,0]=7. If it writes 11 into ordinary destination O1[1,0], that remains 11. The rewrite adds no arithmetic to either result. Output 0 gains a place where a later pass can insert compatible arithmetic before storing. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:89 ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:84

Skipped case: @one_plain has the same [2,2] shape but OutputTensor semantics, so no epilogue is created. Rejected case: if a mapped fused output is not a tensor, lowerToOpaque emits “output fusion is only supported for tensor results.” At creation time intermediateTensor is null; the later accumulation pass assigns its storage source after fusion. These details keep an epilogue closure distinct from an allocated buffer. ↗ opaque-kernels.mlir:37 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:219 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:80

Example 3 · How do fused input roles turn gather's data and indices into load callbacks?

TEST · an opaque gather with exposed access interfaces. opaque-kernels-prologue.mlir starts from mo.gather, imports the test kernel package, then runs --mo-to-map. @gather has data [3,3] f32, indices [2,2] si32, axis 0, and output [2,2,3] f32. Its checks require two input prologues, a rank-3 output epilogue, and axis=0 on the registered call. RUN and expectations Test graph

Illustrative data D = [[0,1,2], [3,4,5], [6,7,8]]   // three source rows
Illustrative indices I = [[2,0], [1,2]]             // four requested row numbers
Expected O = [[[6,7,8], [0,1,2]],                   // I[0,0] and I[0,1]
              [[3,4,5], [6,7,8]]]                  // I[1,0] and I[1,1]
BEFORE · schematic
  %o = mo.gather(%data,%indices) axis=0             // whole-tensor gather operation
  mo.output %o                                    // f32[2,2,3]

AFTER
  %r = map.iter.opaque inputs(%data,%indices)       // outer data dependencies
    outputs(%out:f32[2,2,3]) {                     // local result destination
    %pd = prologue(%di:index<2>) captures(%data) {  // data load interface
      %d = map.load %data[%di]                     // one requested data element
      map.yield %d                                // return scalar to gather
    }
    %pi = prologue(%ii:index<2>) captures(%indices) {// indices load interface
      %n = map.load %indices[%ii]                  // one requested integer index
      map.yield %n                                // return row number to gather
    }
    %eo = epilogue(%v:f32,%oi:index<3>) captures(%out) {
      map.store %out[%oi] = %v                     // retain gather's output coordinate
    }
    map.call.opaque @Gather[axis=0]                // gather's control remains opaque
      inputs(%pd,%pi) outputs(%eo)                 // supply three callbacks
  }
  mo.output %r                                    // result shape is unchanged

buildLoadPrologue constructs a fresh region whose arguments are requested index, captured tensor. The defining statements for its computation are:

Value loaded = MAP::LoadOp::create(builder, loc, inType.getElementType(),
                                   /*tensor=*/cap, /*index=*/idx);
MAP::YieldOp::create(builder, loc, loaded);

The enclosing lowerToOpaque input loop calls this builder only for fused tensor roles. It preserves each input's own rank and scalar element type: the data callback yields f32, the indices callback yields si32. The output callback separately uses rank 3. At output coordinate [0,0,2], the indices callback supplies I[0,0]=2, the data callback supplies D[2,2]=8, and the output callback stores 8. These are illustrative callback values, not operations run by the pass. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:98 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:108 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:111 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:210

QnA 8 · What are `map.iter.opaque` and `map.call.opaque`, what do they do, and how do they support fusion?

map.iter.opaque describes a kernel’s enclosing region and tensor interface. map.call.opaque identifies the Mojo implementation invoked inside that region. Together, they let the compiler work with the kernel’s inputs, outputs and surrounding access paths while retaining its handwritten computation in Mojo.

Operation Main responsibility
map.iter.opaque Own the body region, expose tensor inputs/results, and carry device, dispatch and memory-effect metadata
map.call.opaque Record the selected kernel symbol, compile-time parameters, inputs and output destinations

These roles are defined in the iterator definition and call definition.

Start with your fused-attention graph. Before MO→MAP, the relevant operation is schematically:

%o = mo.custom(%q, %k, %v)
     symbol     = "modular_ops::fused_attention_custom"
     parameters = {BD=8, BN=16}
     device     = gpu:0

mo.output %o

%q, %k, %v, %o : float32[32,32] on gpu:0

This says: apply the registered custom operation to Q, K and V, producing one tensor. MO→MAP replaces that operation with an enclosing iterator and a nested call:

mo.graph @fused_attention
│
├─ graph input arguments
│  ├─ %q : T0
│  ├─ %k : T0
│  └─ %v : T0
│
└─ graph body — relevant operations
   │
   ├─ %o_map = map.iter.opaque
   │  ├─ inputs: %q, %k, %v
   │  ├─ result: %o_map : T0
   │  ├─ device: gpu:0
   │  └─ body region → one block
   │     │
   │     ├─ %qi : T0 ← local Q input
   │     ├─ %ki : T0 ← local K input
   │     ├─ %vi : T0 ← local V input
   │     ├─ %oi : T0 ← local output destination
   │     │
   │     └─ map.call.opaque
   │        ├─ callee: @PKG.fused_attention.FusedAttention
   │        ├─ parameters: {BD=8, BN=16}
   │        ├─ inputs: %qi, %ki, %vi
   │        └─ outputs: %oi
   │
   └─ mo.output %o_map

T0 = float32[32,32] on gpu:0
PKG = illustrative prefix for the imported P1 package

The pass constructs these native IR objects, redirects users of the original result to %o_map, and erases the original mo.custom from IR1. See lowerToOpaque().

Why introduce %qi, %ki and %vi? The iterator’s region has its own local arguments. Each corresponds to an incoming tensor:

Outside the region             Inside the region

%q ──────────────────────────► %qi
%k ──────────────────────────► %ki
%v ──────────────────────────► %vi

Three incoming tensors         Three local names for those inputs

These are different SSA values in different scopes. Introducing local arguments does not copy the tensor contents or add new user inputs. The constructor creates block arguments with the corresponding input types. See body construction.

The fourth local argument, %oi, describes where the kernel writes its result. This is destination-passing style.

Your Mojo implementation accepts an output tensor alongside its three input tensors:

Mojo execute interface, schematically:

execute(
    output,
    query,
    key,
    value,
    context
)

MAP records the corresponding groups as:

map.call.opaque
    inputs (%qi, %ki, %vi)
    outputs(%oi)

Mapping to Mojo parameters:
    %qi → query
    %ki → key
    %vi → value
    %oi → output

The actual signature is at FusedAttention.execute.

Value Meaning
%q, %k, %v Inputs available in the surrounding graph
%qi, %ki, %vi Corresponding inputs available inside the iterator
%oi Destination argument the nested call will write
%o_map Result exposed by the enclosing iterator to subsequent graph operations

For this tensor-result case, the nested call writes %oi; it does not produce another tensor-valued SSA result. The enclosing iterator exposes %o_map. At MAP construction time, %oi is a typed IR argument describing the destination—the construction shown above creates IR, rather than allocating and filling a GPU array.

The nested call also preserves the selected implementation. Its fields answer concrete compiler questions:

Field Attention example Meaning
callee @PKG.fused_attention.FusedAttention Which imported kernel declaration implements the operation?
kernelName "modular_ops::fused_attention_custom" Under which operation name was it registered?
parameters {BD=8, BN=16} Which compile-time choices apply to this call?
inputs %qi, %ki, %vi Which input values does it consume?
outputs %oi Where does it write its tensor result?

The registration name and qualified callee have different purposes: multiple implementation structs can register under one operation name. MAP therefore preserves both. See the call’s attributes and description.

“Opaque” describes the computation boundary. MAP retains the kernel’s declared interface while the internal attention algorithm remains in its Mojo implementation:

Visible to MAP                     Implemented inside Mojo
┌──────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ Inputs: Q, K, V          │       │ Attention algorithm      │
│ Output destination: O    │──────►│ Internal loops and tiles │
│ Parameters: BD, BN       │       │ CPU/GPU implementation   │
│ Selected kernel symbol   │       │ Writes output O          │
└──────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘

Q/K/V/O still have tensor types. The name iter denotes this kernel-region form; the handwritten kernel supplies its internal iteration. For ordinary registered execution kernels, MO→MAP selects this opaque form, while other branches expose elementwise or rowwise computation. See the lowering branches.

A major benefit of the enclosing region is that eligible kernels can expose input-load and output-store callbacks. MAP calls these a prologue and an epilogue:

map.iter.opaque
│
├─ prologue: describe how an input element is obtained
│
├─ map.call.opaque: retain the handwritten kernel computation
│
└─ epilogue: describe how an output element is transformed and stored

A prologue receives an index and yields an input value. An epilogue receives a computed value and index, then transforms or stores it. These interfaces are defined in the callback operations.

For an illustrative output-fusion example, consider matmul followed by bias addition. Assume the selected kernel supports the required output callback and the fusion conditions permit the transformation.

A = [[1,2],           B = [[5,6],
     [3,4]]                [7,8]]

bias = [10,20]

R = matmul(A,B)       # row-by-column products
  = [[19,22],
     [43,50]]

Y = R + bias          # add bias[n] to each element in column n
  = [[29,42],
     [53,70]]

A separate output path could materialize and reread R:

Matmul computes 22 at index (0,1)
                │
                ▼
Store R[0,1] = 22
                │
                ▼
Add operation reads R[0,1] and bias[1]
                │
                ▼
Store Y[0,1] = 22 + 20 = 42

An eligible fused epilogue instead receives the computed value directly:

Matmul computes 22 at index (0,1)
                │
                ▼
Epilogue(value=22, index=(0,1))
├─ load bias[1] → 20
├─ add → 42
└─ store Y[0,1] = 42

The surrounding store path changes while the handwritten matmul computation remains in its implementation. This can avoid the separate intermediate store/read on that fused edge. The source checks conditions such as an existing epilogue and a suitable consumer before performing the rewrite. See fusion checks and the rewrite.

An input prologue provides the corresponding capability on the read side. For an illustrative kernel supporting a fused input callback:

Original expression:
    shifted_A = A + 1
    R = matmul(shifted_A, B)

Example A element:
    A[0,1] = 2
    shifted_A[0,1] = 3

The eligible input path can supply that transformed value when requested:

Kernel requests input at index (0,1)
                │
                ▼
Prologue(index=(0,1))
├─ load A[0,1] → 2
├─ add 1 → 3
└─ yield 3 to the kernel

This illustrates what a supported callback enables; it does not establish that every matmul implementation accepts such fusion. The MO→MAP constructor consults the mapped kernel argument roles before creating load/store callbacks. See fusible argument handling.

Your current attention call uses plain tensor arguments and a plain output destination. Its nested body therefore contains the direct call shown earlier. The prologue/epilogue examples explain capabilities of the representation, rather than transformations automatically applied to this attention kernel.

During the following compiler stage, the two levels lower together:

MAP                                  MOGG
map.iter.opaque ────────────────────► mogg.routine
└─ map.call.opaque ─────────────────► └─ mogg.call.opaque

The routine body introduces pointer arguments and reconstructs typed tensor descriptions. Call lowering also supplies the device context when the selected declaration requires one—as FusedAttention.execute does. These are further compiler transformations toward the eventual Mojo invocation; attention values are computed later during execution. See routine lowering and call/context lowering.

Matched and skipped inputs can coexist. In @partial_fused, only input 0 has a fused role. The test expects one prologue and passes input 1 directly to the call. A plain attention input takes that same direct branch. A fused non-tensor input is rejected before a load closure is constructed. Partial-input test ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:201 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:205

Example 4 · How does tensor addition become one scalar call per tensor index?

SOURCE · different registration branch from attention. adaptor.isElementwise() sends the operation to lowerElementwiseToForeach. The builder requires exactly one tensor result, takes the loop shape from that result type, and creates arguments [inputs…, output, index]. It does not wrap this scalar computation in map.call.opaque. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:724 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:267 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:279 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:293

Inputs A=[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], B=[[10,20,30],[40,50,60]]  // both f32[2,3]

BEFORE · schematic
  %c = mo.add(%a,%b) : f32[2,3]                     // elementwise tensor contract
  mo.output %c                                     // one tensor result

AFTER
  %r = map.iter.elementwise<[2,3]>                  // six logical output coordinates
    inputs(%a as %ai, %b as %bi) outputs(%ci)        // two inputs plus one destination
    index(%i:index<2>) {                           // one coordinate tuple per element
      %av = map.load %ai[%i]                       // A[i]
      %bv = map.load %bi[%i]                       // B[i]
      %cv = map.call.elementwise @Add(%i,%av,%bv)   // scalar Add, returning f32
      map.store %ci[%i] = %cv                      // C[i]
    }
  mo.output %r                                     // [[11,22,33],[44,55,66]]

The native loop inserts one map.load for each MO operand. The call consumes those loaded scalar values and the index, then the store writes the one output argument:

Value scalar = MAP::CallElementwiseOp::create(
    bodyBuilder, loc, elemTy, kernelSymbol, params, idxArg, scalarLoads);

BlockArgument outputArg =
    body->getArgument(static_cast<unsigned>(op->getNumOperands()));
MAP::StoreOp::create(bodyBuilder, loc, outputArg, idxArg, scalar);

At index [1,2], the values are 6+60=66. The operation graph changes from one MO operation to one iterator with four body arguments and four body operations. No memory address is fixed at this point. The source uses each input tensor's element type for its load and the result tensor's element type for the scalar result, so dtype-changing elementwise registrations can use the same builder. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:303 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:317

TEST · direct entry at MO. elementwise-add-static.mlir supplies [8,16,128] operands, imports built-ins, and runs --mo-to-map. Lines 18–22 require the result-shaped iterator, two loads at the same captured index, .Add, and a store. CHECK-NOT excludes an opaque iterator, and the end-of-line check confirms the default deferred dispatch is omitted from printing. The [2,3] arrays above are a smaller illustration of that same lowering. ↗ elementwise-add-static.mlir:1 ↗ elementwise-add-static.mlir:6 ↗ elementwise-add-static.mlir:16

Guard: zero or multiple results, or a non-tensor result, cause explicit diagnostics in this elementwise builder. Broadcasting is represented through the separate broadcast view branch below; this example's two operands already have equal shapes. Attention's ordinary execute declaration does not match isElementwise(). ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:267 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:271 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:749 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:74

Example 5 · How does a transpose expose its index mapping and retain its launch policy?

TEST · standalone transpose, already supplied as MO. transpose-view.mlir imports built-ins and runs --mo-to-map; its @transposeSwap input is exactly [2,3] → [3,2] with permutation [1,0]. CHECK expects a result-shaped elementwise iterator, dispatch(immediate), an index transpose, a load at the transformed index and a store at the original index. RUN Input and expectation

Input X=[[0,1,2],[3,4,5]]                           // row-major f32[2,3]

BEFORE · schematic
  %perm = mo.constant [1,0] : si64[2]              // output-axis to input-axis mapping
  %t = mo.transpose(%x,%perm) : f32[3,2]           // tensor-level transpose
  mo.output %t                                    // [[0,3],[1,4],[2,5]]

AFTER
  %perm = mo.constant [1,0] : si64[2]              // remains an explicit input value
  %r = map.iter.elementwise<[3,2]> dispatch(immediate)
    inputs(%x as %xi,%perm as %pi) outputs(%o)      // two input arguments, one destination
    index(%i:index<2>) {                           // coordinate in the output
      %j = map.index.transpose<[2,3]->[3,2],perm=[1,0]>(%i,%pi)
                                                   // [i0,i1] maps to [i1,i0]
      %v = map.load %xi[%j]                        // load original input coordinate
      map.store %o[%i] = %v                        // write corresponding output coordinate
    }
  mo.output %r                                    // same elements, transposed shape

The implementation creates the index op and wires its result only to the input load:

Value innerIdx = MAP::TransposeIndexOp::create(
    bodyBuilder, loc, MAP::IndexType::get(ctx, rank), spec, idxArg, permArg);
Value loaded = MAP::LoadOp::create(
    bodyBuilder, loc, outputTy.getElementType(), inputArg, innerIdx);
MAP::StoreOp::create(bodyBuilder, loc, outputArg, idxArg, loaded);

At output [2,1], input [1,2] has row-major offset 1×3+2=5 elements, or 20 bytes from the input base for f32. The new output has its own logical offset 2×2+1=5; equal offsets here are incidental to this coordinate. At output [1,0], input [0,1] has offset 1, while the output offset is 2. This is an index rewrite; later passes decide whether a strided view can replace part of the representation. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:633

Static versus dynamic branch. A constant permutation is copied into TransposeSpecAttr; otherwise the spec contains ? entries and the permutation tensor remains the source of the runtime values. The test's @transposeDynamicPerm checks that dynamic permutation still takes the view-index route. A rank-changing transpose is rejected. stampAsyncLaunch selects immediate dispatch because the source operation is MO::TransposeOp. Dynamic test ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:598 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:602 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:619 ↗ MOUtils.cpp:27

This separate graph transpose is not the Kᵀ calculation inside P1's fused-attention implementation. The actual attention graph has no mo.transpose edge for this pass to inspect. ↗ fused_attention.py:57 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:346

Example 6 · How do broadcast and reshape change index rank while preserving their tensor contracts?

SOURCE · both loops visit output coordinates. lowerBroadcastToForeach and lowerReshapeToForeach create a loop index with the output rank, then an index-transform result with the input rank. The view signature stores both shapes. Broadcast projects repeated coordinates; reshape preserves a row-major linear position. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:486 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:518 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:525 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:538 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:575

BROADCAST · schematic, B=[10,20,30] : f32[3]
  BEFORE %o = mo.static.broadcast_to(%b) : f32[2,3] // repeat the input vector twice
  AFTER  %o = map.iter.elementwise<[2,3]>           // six output positions
           inputs(%b) outputs(%out) index(%i:index<2>) {
             %j = map.index.broadcast<[3]->[2,3]>(%i) // [row,col] → [col]
             %v = map.load %b[%j]                     // rank-1 input access
             map.store %out[%i] = %v                  // rank-2 output access
           }
  OUTPUT [[10,20,30],[10,20,30]]                    // B[2]=30 supplies both rows

RESHAPE · schematic, X=[[0,1,2],[3,4,5]] : f32[2,3]
  BEFORE %o = mo.static.reshape(%x) : f32[6]        // flatten while preserving order
  AFTER  %o = map.iter.elementwise<[6]>             // six rank-1 output positions
           inputs(%x) outputs(%out) index(%i:index<1>) {
             %j = map.index.reshape<[2,3]->[6]>(%i) // [k] → [k/3,k%3]
             %v = map.load %x[%j]                   // rank-2 input access
             map.store %out[%i] = %v                // rank-1 output access
           }
  OUTPUT [0,1,2,3,4,5]                            // position 4 reads X[1,1]=4

These are the two native index-construction statements:

Value innerIdx = MAP::BroadcastIndexOp::create(
    bodyBuilder, loc, MAP::IndexType::get(ctx, inRank), spec, idxArg);
Value innerIdx = MAP::ReshapeIndexOp::create(
    bodyBuilder, loc, MAP::IndexType::get(ctx, inRank), spec, idxArg);

Each is followed by a load at innerIdx and a store at idxArg. Each iterator has one tensor input, one destination and one index argument; it does not acquire runtime dimension tensors merely because the two ranks differ. In the reshape example, index [4] and index [1,1] both refer to linear position 4, or 16 bytes from a row-major f32 base. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:513 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:525 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:563 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:575

TEST · two independent MO inputs. broadcast-view.mlir runs import + --mo-to-map on [64] → [8,64]; lines 28–39 check a rank-2 loop and rank-1 input index. reshape-view.mlir runs the same passes on [4,6] → [24]; lines 10–21 check a rank-1 loop and a reshape index used by the input load. These tests enter before MO→MAP and stop before later view fusion or contiguous-view raising. Broadcast RUN Broadcast expectations Reshape RUN Reshape expectations

Guard: the broadcast builder rejects input rank greater than output rank. Reshape permits rank changes in either direction and assumes a valid reshape contract; it does not infer -1 here. A rank-0 scalar 9 broadcast to [4,7] therefore denotes 28 values equal to 9: every rank-2 output coordinate projects to the scalar's empty input index. That is illustrative broadcast arithmetic, not a captured test dump. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:495 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:536 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:525

Example 7 · How are slice bounds normalized and connected to the generated load?

TEST · reverse slice with known bounds. slice-view.mlir imports built-ins and runs --mo-to-map. @sliceReverseStep supplies an input [10,64], start [-1,32], stop [-7,64], step [-2,1], and output [3,32]. Its expected MAP spec contains normalized starts [9,32], stops [3,64], and unchanged steps [-2,1]. RUN Reverse-slice input and CHECK

BEFORE · schematic, X[r,c]=100*r+c on f32[10,64]
  %start = mo.constant [-1,32] : si64[2]           // Python-style negative first bound
  %stop  = mo.constant [-7,64] : si64[2]           // exclusive stop
  %step  = mo.constant [-2,1] : si64[2]            // reverse rows, forward columns
  %o = mo.slice(%x,%start,%stop,%step) : f32[3,32]  // rows 9,7,5; columns 32…63
  mo.output %o                                    // retain selected elements

AFTER
  %o = map.iter.elementwise<[3,32]>                // iterate 96 output coordinates
    inputs(%x,%start,%stop,%step) outputs(%out) index(%i:index<2>) {
      %j = map.index.slice<starts=[9,32],stops=[3,64],steps=[-2,1]>
        (%i,%start,%stop,%step)                    // [r,c] → [9-2*r,32+c]
      %v = map.load %x[%j]                         // selected original element
      map.store %out[%i] = %v                      // compact output coordinate
    }
  mo.output %o                                    // same selected data

The normalization uses the static input dimension and the sign of the static step:

int64_t lo = steps[i] > 0 ? 0 : -1;
int64_t hi = steps[i] > 0 ? dim : dim - 1;
auto normalize = [&](int64_t v) {
  if (ShapedType::isDynamic(v))
    return v;
  return std::clamp<int64_t>(v < 0 ? v + dim : v, lo, hi);
};
starts[i] = normalize(starts[i]);
stops[i] = normalize(stops[i]);

For the first dimension, dim=10: -1+10=9, -7+10=3; the reverse walk visits 9,7,5 and stops before 3. At output [2,0], the input coordinate is [5,32], the illustrative value is 532, and the input offset is 5×64+32=352 elements (1408 bytes for f32). The four input operands remain; normalized literals enrich the spec rather than replacing those SSA operands. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:410 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:424 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:457 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:471

Matched and skipped normalization. boundsOrDynamic treats each complete start/stop/step tensor independently. A graph-argument step yields steps=[?,?] even when starts/stops are constants; when the step or dimension is dynamic, the normalization loop skips that dimension. The test @sliceNonConstantStep checks this mixed case. Rank changes are rejected, and SliceSpecAttr::verify runs before the spec is constructed. Mixed-bound CHECK ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:398 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:402 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:418 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:435

Example 8 · How does a reduction registration become a rowwise iterator with a nested fold?

SOURCE · monoid registration selects this branch. lowerOp tests isReduction() before isElementwise() or the ordinary execute path. lowerReductionToRowwise derives the reduction axis from the input and result shapes, creates one rowwise iterator, then a nested map.iter.reduce that names the registered monoid. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:717 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:646 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:662 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:682

Input X=[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] : f32[2,3]               // two rows to reduce

BEFORE · schematic
  %s = mo.reduce.add(%x) : f32[2,3] -> f32[2,1]    // axis 1 shrinks to size 1
  mo.output %s                                    // [[6],[15]]

AFTER
  %s = map.iter.rowwise<[2,3], axis=1>             // reduction domain stays [2,3]
    inputs(%x as %xi) outputs(%out:f32[2,1])
    row(%row:index<2>) {                           // identifies the destination row
      %sum = map.iter.reduce @ReduceSum            // registered reduction semantics
        index(%i:index<2>) -> f32 {                // index ranges over this row's inputs
          %v = map.load %xi[%i]                    // one input element
          map.yield %v                            // feed the reduction monoid
        }
      map.store %out[%row] = %sum                  // one scalar result per row
    }
  mo.output %s                                    // same rank-preserving result

The fold body has one index argument and yields a loaded input element. The surrounding body holds the input, output destination(s), and row index. Scalar output types come from the element types of the original tensor results:

SmallVector<Type> foldTypes;
for (Type resultTy : op->getResultTypes())
  foldTypes.push_back(cast<MO::TensorType>(resultTy).getElementType());

After constructing the reduction op, the builder pairs each destination with its corresponding returned field:

for (auto [outputArg, field] :
     llvm::zip_equal(outputArgs, reduceOp.getResults()))
  MAP::StoreOp::create(bodyBuilder, loc, outputArg, rowArg, field);

For the illustrative first row, the sum is 1+2+3=6; for the second it is 15. The builder records the monoid symbol rather than spelling a sequential addition tree, so this representation does not promise a particular floating-point reduction order. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:677 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:685 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:695

The same file's @argMax supplies two tensor results and expects fold fields (bf16,si64) with two stores, preserving value and index outputs separately. RUN and sum expectation ArgMax expectation

Guard: an invalid axis inferred from the type contract returns an error. An ordinary opaque registration does not enter this branch merely because its authored implementation performs reductions. P1's attention softmax therefore remains inside P1. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:648 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:718 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:74

TEST · mutation has a different contract. elementwise-kernels.mlir imports the test kernel package and runs only --mo-to-map. @mutable_store supplies a buffer [2,2], two tensors [2,2], a chain creator, an add and a store. Its checks require two separate elementwise iterators; the store iterator has outputs (), a chain result, an identity MutableStore scalar call, a buffer store and hasWriteEffect=true. RUN Input and expectations

Inputs A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[10,20],[30,40]]        // both f32[2,2]
Existing BUF has shape [2,2]                     // destination already belongs to caller

BEFORE · schematic

  %sum = mo.add(%a,%b)                           // [[11,22],[33,44]]
  %c1 = mo.mutable.store(%buf,%sum,%c0)           // update BUF; result is !mo.chain

AFTER
  %sum = map.iter.elementwise<[2,2]> {           // independent Add iterator

    %bv = map.load %b[%i]                        // load B at iterator index

/*resultTypes=*/SmallVector<Type>{MO::ChainType::get(ctx)},
/*shape=*/shapeAttr,
/*inputs=*/ValueRange{op.getInTensor(), op.getInBuffer()},
/*chain=*/op.getInChain(),

These are arguments to IterElementwiseOp::create. The body has only [tensor value, buffer, index]; it receives neither an output-tensor argument nor a chain argument. The store targets bufferArg, while users of the old chain result are redirected to the new iterator result. ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:711 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:340 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:347 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:359 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:379

QnA 9 · What does “runtime” mean here?

Yes—“runtime” here means the MAX execution/runtime side, but more specifically, it means the tensor-shape representation that execution supports. It doesn’t mean the whole MAX framework, and it doesn’t mean a tensor is already running when this check happens.

The compiler checks the rank during compilation because later execution structures have to represent the tensor. In this checkout, kMaxRank is 8; the comment says it must match the rank limit used by the Mojo Buffer type. So MO→MAP rejects a known rank above 8 before lowering it into representations that cannot support it.

For example, float32[32,32] has rank 2 and passes this check. A tensor with nine axes has rank 9 and triggers the compile error. The MAX repository includes both MAX and Mojo, which is why the compiler and execution-side limit are coordinated. (github.com)

QnA 10 · What do `Operation*`, preserved MO op and eligible MO operation mean?

These lines describe a compile-time scan of IR1, not execution of the tensor operations. The scan decides which operation nodes MO→MAP should attempt to lower.

An MLIR Operation is one node in the in-memory IR: it has a name, operands, results, attributes, and possibly regions. So Operation* is a C++ pointer to that node. It is not a pointer to tensor data and not a Python TensorValue. The worklist stores the pointers temporarily so the pass can visit the selected IR nodes after the scan. MLIR’s IR is nested as operations containing regions, regions containing blocks, and blocks containing operations. (mlir.llvm.org) The worklist is built in MOToMAP.cpp:767.

“Preserved MO op” means MO→MAP leaves that operation in the MO form. The operation is still visited, but shouldLower does not add it to this pass’s worklist. “Preserved” means preserved during this lowering step; a later pass may handle it. For example, mo.graph and mo.output are preserved. mo.constant and mo.transfer are examples too. The predicate is in MOToMAP.cpp:63; the operation definitions show the preservation marker, for example mo.graph and mo.constant.

“Eligible MO operation” means a candidate for MO→MAP. It must be an MO-dialect operation, must not have the preservation marker, must not be mo.invoke_shape_func, and must pass the rank check. Eligible means “put it on the worklist,” not “a rewrite is guaranteed.” The pass still needs to find a registered implementation and choose a lowering path. mo.custom is an example: the fused-attention custom op is rank 2, so it is eligible and MO→MAP attempts to turn it into map.iter.opaque with a nested map.call.opaque. The rank check and worklist insertion are in MOToMAP.cpp:773–780.

Here’s a simplified view of the scan:

builtin.module                         → not an MO op; not added
└─ mo.graph                            → preserved container; walk continues inside
   ├─ mo.constant                      → preserved for this pass
   ├─ mo.custom(%q, %k, %v)            → eligible; save its Operation* in worklist
   └─ mo.output %result                → preserved for this pass

After the scan:
worklist ──► try lowering the saved mo.custom node

mo.invoke_shape_func is a special exclusion: this pass skips it because it has no MAP form; the source says it is lowered by MAP→MOGG. In contrast, if a registered implementation cannot be found for an otherwise eligible operation, MO→MAP can leave that operation unchanged. So the worklist is a list of candidates, not a list of already-transformed operations.

QnA 11 · What does “registration key” mean for MO→MAP?

A registration key is the exact string the compiler uses to find the Mojo kernel declaration that implements an operation. For fused attention, that key is:

modular_ops::fused_attention_custom

The value flows through the compiler like this:

Python ops.custom(name="modular_ops::fused_attention_custom", ...)
        │
        └─ stored on mo.custom as its symbol string
                 │
                 └─ getMojoOperationInfo(customOp)
                       → operationName = "modular_ops::fused_attention_custom"
                       → function label = "execute"
                              │
                              └─ MojoRegistry lookup by operationName
                                    → matching FusedAttention declaration
                                    → resolve for the op's device

The Python call creates a StringAttr from name and attaches it to mo.custom as symbol. The Mojo package uses the same string in @register("modular_ops::fused_attention_custom") on FusedAttention. So the registry can match the recorded operation to that declaration. The same registration string appears in the public fused-attention example. (github.com)

In the call stack, getMojoOperationInfo extracts that symbol for a custom op. MojoRegistry stores declarations under their registration strings, then looks up the key and resolves a matching declaration for the operation’s device. For this example, the device is GPU 0, and the selected declaration exposes its execute function. Python custom-op construction · key extraction and lookup · registry entries · attention registration

The key is just the lookup name. It isn’t the FusedAttention type name, the execute method name, the Q/K/V operands, the BD/BN parameters, or the device. Those are obtained or checked separately. The :: is part of the literal key; the registry looks up the whole string. For non-custom MO operations, the lookup name generally comes from the operation’s registered name instead.

QnA 12 · How does MO→MAP know whether a registered kernel is reduction, elementwise or ordinary execute?

Correct: no earlier step adds a reduction or elementwise flag to the MO operation itself. The MO operation carries information such as its registration symbol and device. MO→MAP uses those to find the kernel declaration, then classifies the declaration.

P1 Mojo package
  @register("modular_ops::fused_attention_custom")
  struct FusedAttention { execute(...) }
          │
          ▼ package import records a kernel declaration
separate KernelDeclOp in the kernel registry
  execute = present
  elementwise = absent
  reduction = absent
          │
          ▼ MO operation's symbol + device select that declaration
KernelDeclAdaptor
  isReduction()   → reduction metadata exists?
  isElementwise() → elementwise function exists?

In lowerOp, MO→MAP first calls getMojoKernelAdaptor. For a custom MO op, lookup uses its symbol; it resolves the matching kernel for the op’s device and builds an adaptor from that declaration. Then isReduction() and isElementwise() simply check whether the corresponding optional metadata exists. MOToMAP.cpp Support.cpp KernelDeclAdaptor.h

The package importer fills that declaration metadata while scanning Mojo kernels: it records an elementwise entry point when present, and records reduction metadata when the kernel conforms to ReduceOp. The adaptor later copies those fields from the declaration. ImportPackages.cpp KernelDeclAdaptor.cpp

For the examples:

  • Reduction: OnlineLogSumExp conforms to ReduceOp, so its imported declaration has reduction metadata and isReduction() is true. monoids.mojo
  • Elementwise: AddOneElementwise declares an elementwise method, so its declaration has an elementwise function and isElementwise() is true. add_one.mojo
  • Fused attention: FusedAttention declares execute, not an elementwise entry point or ReduceOp conformance. Both checks are false; the execute function is used, and this custom op proceeds through the ordinary execute lowering path. fused_attention.mojo

So an operation that mathematically performs a reduction is not necessarily classified as a reduction here. The branch follows how its registered kernel is declared. Earlier graph-building and verification can make the package declaration available and validate the call, but they do not stamp a reduction flag onto the MO op.

// Base class for ops in this dialect.
class MAP_Op<string mnemonic, list<Trait> traits = []>
    : Op<MAPDialect, mnemonic, traits>;

// Type constraint matching the `map.index<N>` type.
def MAP_AnyIndex : Type<
    CPred<"::llvm::isa<::M::MAP::IndexType>($_self)">,
    "map.index type">;

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.opaque
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterOpaqueOp : MAP_Op<"iter.opaque", [
    AttrSizedOperandSegments,
    IsolatedFromAbove,
    MAP_IterOpInterface,
    SingleBlock,
    NoTerminator,
    MO_ExplicitDevice,
    MO_HasDeviceInterface,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<OpAsmOpInterface, ["getAsmBlockArgumentNames"]>,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MemoryEffectsOpInterface>,
  ]> {
  let summary = "An opaque (hand-written) kernel with fusible load/store paths.";
  let description = [{
    Wraps a call to an opaque Mojo kernel (e.g. a hand-tuned GEMM) that exposes
    named load/store callbacks. The body holds the load/store callbacks
    (`map.iter.prologue` / `map.iter.epilogue`) plus the `map.call.opaque` that
    invokes the kernel; it is not a sequence of computation ops.

    The region is isolated from above: `inputs` and `outputs` are shadowed as
    body block arguments. Outputs are destination-passing, so the body needs no
    terminator unless a `map.call.opaque` returns a by-value result, which
    `map.yield` carries out.

    ```mlir
    %mm = map.iter.opaque
        inputs (%A : !mo.tensor<[M, K], bf16>, %B : !mo.tensor<[K, N], bf16>)
        outputs (%out : !mo.tensor<[M, N], bf16>) {
      %epi = map.iter.epilogue (%val : bf16, %idx : !map.index<2>) capturing {%cap = %out : !mo.tensor<[M, N], bf16>} {
        map.store %cap[%idx] = %val : !mo.tensor<[M, N], bf16>
      } : !mo.tensor<[M, N], bf16>
      map.call.opaque @builtin_kernels.linalg.Matmul[transpose_b = false]
        inputs (%A, %B) outputs (%epi) : (...) -> (...)
    }
    ```

    A mutating kernel takes an `!mo.chain` through `$inputChain` and returns
    one as the trailing result. The chain is pure sequencing: it has no block
    argument and never reaches the `map.call.opaque`.

    `hasReadEffect`/`hasWriteEffect` carry forward the original op's memory
    effects instead of the conservative "unknown effects" default.

    `fusionInfo` records the kernel's fusion-tree provenance (a `mogg.fusion`
    attribute), typed `AnyAttr` so `map` need not depend on `mogg`.

    The execution device is an explicit `#M.device_ref` (`MO_ExplicitDevice`)
    rather than inferred from types as on `map.iter.elementwise`: inference cannot
    tell "runs on the host" from "don't know" for unannotated tensors, which
    matters for passes that must refuse to act on device kernels.
  }];

  let arguments = (ins
    Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer, MO_Opaque]>>:$inputs,
    Optional<MO_Chain>:$inputChain,
    OptionalAttr<AnyAttr>:$fusionInfo,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasReadEffect,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasWriteEffect,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<MOGG_DispatchKindAttr,
                              "::M::MOGG::DispatchKind::Deferred">:$dispatch
  );
  let results = (outs Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Opaque, MO_Chain]>>:$results);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let extraClassDeclaration = [{
    /// The number of results that have a body block argument. `$results` is
    /// ordered [DPS results..., by-value opaque?, chain?]; only the DPS ones
    /// have one.
    unsigned getNumNonChainResults();

    /// The by-value `!mo.opaque` result, or null when there is none.
    ::mlir::Value getOpaqueResult();

    /// The trailing `getNumNonChainResults()` body block arguments (block
    /// arguments are ordered [non-chain inputs..., DPS outputs...]).
    ::mlir::Block::BlockArgListType getOutputBlockArgs();

    /// The body block arguments shadowing `$inputs`, one-to-one.
    ::mlir::Block::BlockArgListType getInputBlockArgs();

    /// Returns the `$inputs` operand `arg` shadows, or null when `arg` shadows
    /// none (e.g. an output block arg). The inverse of `getInputBlockArgs()`.
    ::mlir::Value getInputFor(::mlir::BlockArgument arg);

    /// The `map.iter.epilogue` wrapping DPS result `resultIdx` -- the one that
    /// captures its output block arg -- or null when that result has none.
    IterEpilogueOp getEpilogueForResult(unsigned resultIdx);

    /// Inserts `vals` as new (non-chain) inputs starting at `idx`, updating
    /// both operands and the corresponding shadowed body block arguments.
    void insertInputsAt(unsigned idx, ::mlir::ValueRange vals);

    /// Erases a range of (non-chain) inputs at `[idx, idx + len)`, updating
    /// both operands and the corresponding shadowed body block arguments.
    void eraseInputsAt(unsigned idx, size_t len = 1);

    /// Returns the output chain (always the last result), or null.
    ::mlir::Value getOutputChain();

    /// Sets the input chain operand. No-op when `chain` is null. Requires a
    /// chain input to already exist.
    void setChain(::mlir::Value chain);
  }];

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;
  let hasCanonicalizer = 1;
}

def MAP_YieldOp : MAP_Op<"yield", [Terminator]> {
  let summary = "Terminates a map.iter.opaque body, yielding its results.";
  let description = [{
    Terminates a `map.iter.prologue`, a `map.iter.reduce` (yielding its
    contribution), or a `map.iter.opaque` body whose `map.call.opaque` returns
    a by-value result.
  }];

  let arguments = (ins Variadic<AnyType>:$operands);

  let assemblyFormat = "($operands^ `:` type($operands))? attr-dict";
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.epilogue
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterEpilogueOp : MAP_Op<"iter.epilogue", [
    IsolatedFromAbove,
    SingleBlock,
    NoTerminator,
    AttrSizedOperandSegments,
    MAP_CapturingFusionClosure,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<OpAsmOpInterface, ["getAsmBlockArgumentNames"]>,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
  ]> {
  let summary = "A store-path callback inlined into an opaque kernel's output.";
  let description = [{
    An SSA callback the enclosing `map.call.opaque` consumes on its `outputs`:
    it is handed a value and an index and stores (or transforms then stores)
    it. The leading block arguments are the value and the index; the rest
    shadow the captured operands. The `capturing {...}` clause is print/parse
    sugar over those operands.

    `$intermediateTensor` (not a capture, so no block argument) is the tensor
    whose base pointer the kernel-facing epilogue slice is built over. Set by
    `AllocateAccumulatingBuffers`.
  }];

  let arguments = (ins
    Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>>:$captures,
    Optional<AnyType>:$intermediateTensor
  );
  let results = (outs AnyType:$result);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasCanonicalizer = 1;
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.prologue
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterPrologueOp : MAP_Op<"iter.prologue", [
    IsolatedFromAbove,
    SingleBlock,
    MAP_CapturingFusionClosure,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<OpAsmOpInterface, ["getAsmBlockArgumentNames"]>,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
  ]> {
  let summary = "A load-path callback inlined into an opaque kernel's input.";
  let description = [{
    An SSA callback the enclosing `map.call.opaque` consumes on its `inputs`:
    it is handed an index and yields the value the kernel reads there. The
    leading block argument is the index; the rest shadow the captured operands.
    The `capturing {...}` clause is print/parse sugar over those operands.
  }];

  let arguments = (ins Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>>:$captures);
  let results = (outs AnyType:$result);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasCanonicalizer = 1;
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.call
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_ConstantOp : MAP_Op<"constant", [
    ConstantLike,
    Pure,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
  ]> {
  let summary = "A constant folded into a kernel body.";
  let description = [{
    Carries an `mo.constant` that `FuseConstantIterOpaqueInputs` folded into a
    `map.iter.opaque` body. A clone of the `mo.constant` cannot be used: the
    body must hold only `LowerableToMOGGInterface` ops, and `mo` cannot
    implement it without depending on `mogg`.
  }];
  let arguments = (ins ElementsAttr:$value);
  let results = (outs MO_Tensor:$result);
  let assemblyFormat = [{ $value attr-dict `:` type($result) }];
  // `ConstantLike` requires a folder returning the constant's value.
  let hasFolder = 1;
}

def MAP_CallOpaqueOp : MAP_Op<"call.opaque", [
    AttrSizedOperandSegments,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<SymbolUserOpInterface>,
    DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
  ]> {
  let summary = "Invoke an opaque Mojo kernel by symbol.";
  let description = [{
    Calls the kernel declared under `callee` (a `mogg.kernel.decl` symbol, e.g.
    `@builtin_kernels.linalg.Matmul`) with the given `inputs` and `outputs`. The
    kernel parameters (e.g. `packed_b`, `transpose_b`) are carried in brackets
    immediately after the callee symbol, e.g.
    `@...Matmul[packed_b = false, transpose_b = false]`.

    `kernelName` is the callee's `registration` (e.g. `mo.matmul`). Several
    structs may register under one name, so it cannot be derived from
    `callee`. Passes that need the implemented MO op match on it, so renaming
    a Mojo struct cannot change their behavior.
  }];

  let arguments = (ins
    FlatSymbolRefAttr:$callee,
    StrAttr:$kernelName,
    DictionaryAttr:$params,
    Variadic<AnyType>:$inputs,
    Variadic<AnyType>:$outputs,
    // The source op's `MO_SameVariadicOperandSize` trait, so `mogg.call.opaque`
    // can split the flat operands into equal-length variadic groups.
    DefaultValuedAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasSameVariadicOperandSize
  );

  // A by-value result, with no `$outputs` entry; carried out by `map.yield`.
  let results = (outs Optional<MO_Opaque>:$opaqueResult);

  let hasVerifier = 1;

  let assemblyFormat = [{
    $callee `[` custom<KernelParamsBody>($params) `]`
    `inputs` `(` $inputs `)` `outputs` `(` $outputs `)`
    (`returns` type($opaqueResult)^)?
    `kernelName` `=` $kernelName
    (`hasSameVariadicOperandSize` `=` $hasSameVariadicOperandSize^)?
    attr-dict `:` functional-type($inputs, $outputs)
  }];
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.elementwise
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterElementwiseOp : MAP_Op<"iter.elementwise", [
  AttrSizedOperandSegments,
  IsolatedFromAbove,
  MAP_IterOpInterface,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MAP_StructuredIterOpInterface>,
  SingleBlock,
  NoTerminator,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MO_HasDeviceInterface>,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MemoryEffectsOpInterface>,
]> {
  let summary = "Structured iteration over a tensor shape";
  let description = [{
    Iterates over every point in an N-dimensional shape, executing the body
    region once per index. The shape is a `MOSH::ShapeAttr` and may contain
    static integer dims, named symbolic parameters (D0, D1, …), or parametric
    expressions.

    Inputs (tensors or, for in-place kernels, buffers) are shadowed as body
    block arguments. Outputs are extra block arguments matching the non-chain
    results. Block arguments are ordered [inputs..., outputs..., index].

    The optional `chain` operand/result models mutating kernels (e.g.
    `mo.mutable.store`). It has no block argument, and the output chain is
    always the last result.

    `hasReadEffect`/`hasWriteEffect` carry forward the original op's memory
    effects instead of the conservative "unknown effects" default.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %result = map.iter.elementwise<[8, 16, 128]>
        inputs  (%x: !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>,
                 %y: !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>)
        outputs (%out: !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>)
        index   (%idx: !map.index<3>)
        -> !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>
    { ... }
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins
    MOSH_ShapeAttr:$shape,
    Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>>:$inputs,
    Optional<MO_Chain>:$chain,
    OptionalAttr<MOGG_FusionInfoAttr>:$fusionInfo,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasReadEffect,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasWriteEffect,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<MOGG_DispatchKindAttr,
                              "::M::MOGG::DispatchKind::Deferred">:$dispatch
  );

  let results = (outs Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Chain]>>:$results);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;

  let extraClassDeclaration = [{
    ::mlir::Block::BlockArgListType getInputBlockArgs();
    ::mlir::Block::BlockArgListType getOutputBlockArgs();

    // Inserts/erases inputs along with their body block arguments.
    void insertInputsAt(unsigned idx, ValueRange vals);
    void eraseInputsAt(unsigned idx, size_t len = 1);

    Value getInputChain() { return getChain(); }
    // Null if the last result isn't a chain.
    Value getOutputChain();
    // No-op when `chain` is null.
    void setChain(Value chain);
  }];
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.elementwise.body
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterElementwiseBodyOp : MAP_Op<"iter.elementwise.body", [
  HasParent<"IterOpaqueOp">,
  IsolatedFromAbove,
  SingleBlock,
  NoTerminator,
  MAP_CapturingFusionClosure,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
]> {
  let summary = "The per-index body of a structured MAP loop, wrapped for outlining.";
  let description = [{
    Holds the per-index computation of a `map.iter.elementwise` after
    `OutlineStructuredKernelBodies` wraps it in a `map.iter.opaque`. The
    opaque's input and output block arguments are its `$captures` (see
    `CapturingFusionClosure`); the leading block argument is the index.
    `shape` is copied from the wrapped `map.iter.elementwise`.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %r = map.iter.opaque
        inputs (%x: !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>, %y: !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>)
        outputs (%out: !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>) {
      map.iter.elementwise.body<[8, 16, 128]>
          index (%idx: !map.index<3>)
          capturing {%x0 = %x, %y0 = %y, %out0 = %out} {
        %xv = map.load %x0[%idx] : !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>
        %yv = map.load %y0[%idx] : !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>
        %sum = map.call.elementwise @builtin_kernels.elementwise.Add(%idx, %xv, %yv)
                  : !map.index<3>, f32, f32 -> f32
        map.store %out0[%idx] = %sum : !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>
      }
    }
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins MOSH_ShapeAttr:$shape,
                       Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>>:$captures);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasCanonicalizer = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.rowwise
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterRowwiseOp : MAP_Op<"iter.rowwise", [
  AttrSizedOperandSegments,
  IsolatedFromAbove,
  MAP_IterOpInterface,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MAP_StructuredIterOpInterface>,
  SingleBlock,
  NoTerminator,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MO_HasDeviceInterface>,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<MemoryEffectsOpInterface>,
]> {
  let summary = "A kernel that runs its body once per row of a shape";
  let description = [{
    Iterates over the rows of `shape` along `axis`. The body runs once per row
    and holds the row's phases in order: folds (`map.iter.reduce`), row-scalar
    ops on their results, and stores.

    The row index `%row` indexes the per-row space, `shape` with the `axis`
    coordinate pinned to 0, so it addresses a per-row (`axis` size 1) output
    directly. Each result is per-row or has the full `shape`.

    Inputs (tensors or, for in-place kernels, buffers) are shadowed as body
    block arguments. Outputs are extra block arguments matching the non-chain
    results. Block arguments are ordered [inputs..., outputs..., row].

    As on `map.iter.elementwise`, the optional `chain` operand/result models
    mutating kernels; it has no block argument, and the output chain is always
    the last result. `hasReadEffect`/`hasWriteEffect` carry forward the
    original op's memory effects instead of the conservative "unknown effects"
    default, and `dispatch` prints only when it isn't `deferred`.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %sum = map.iter.rowwise<[M, N], axis = 1>
        inputs  (%x: !mo.tensor<[M, N], f32>)
        outputs (%out: !mo.tensor<[M, 1], f32>)
        row     (%row: !map.index<2>) -> !mo.tensor<[M, 1], f32> {
      %acc = map.iter.reduce @builtin_kernels.monoids.ReduceSum
          index (%i: !map.index<2>) -> f32 {
        %v = map.load %x[%i] : !mo.tensor<[M, N], f32>
        map.yield %v : f32
      }
      map.store %out[%row] = %acc : !mo.tensor<[M, 1], f32>
    }
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins
    MOSH_ShapeAttr:$shape,
    I64Attr:$axis,
    Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>>:$inputs,
    Optional<MO_Chain>:$chain,
    OptionalAttr<MOGG_FusionInfoAttr>:$fusionInfo,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasReadEffect,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<BoolAttr, "false">:$hasWriteEffect,
    DefaultValuedOptionalAttr<MOGG_DispatchKindAttr,
                              "::M::MOGG::DispatchKind::Deferred">:$dispatch
  );

  let results = (outs Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Chain]>>:$results);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;

  let extraClassDeclaration = [{
    ::mlir::Block::BlockArgListType getInputBlockArgs();
    ::mlir::Block::BlockArgListType getOutputBlockArgs();
    ::mlir::BlockArgument getRowArg();

    // Inserts/erases inputs along with their body block arguments.
    void insertInputsAt(unsigned idx, ::mlir::ValueRange vals);
    void eraseInputsAt(unsigned idx, size_t len = 1);

    ::mlir::Value getInputChain() { return getChain(); }
    // Null if the last result isn't a chain.
    ::mlir::Value getOutputChain();
    // No-op when `chain` is null.
    void setChain(::mlir::Value chain);
  }];
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.rowwise.body
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterRowwiseBodyOp : MAP_Op<"iter.rowwise.body", [
  HasParent<"IterOpaqueOp">,
  IsolatedFromAbove,
  SingleBlock,
  NoTerminator,
  MAP_CapturingFusionClosure,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
]> {
  let summary = "The per-row body of a map.iter.rowwise, wrapped for outlining.";
  let description = [{
    Holds the per-row computation of a `map.iter.rowwise` after
    `OutlineStructuredKernelBodies` wraps it in a `map.iter.opaque`, as
    `map.iter.elementwise.body` does for `map.iter.elementwise`. The opaque's input and
    output block arguments are its `$captures` (see `CapturingFusionClosure`);
    the leading block argument is the row index. `shape` and `axis` are copied
    from the wrapped `map.iter.rowwise`.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %r = map.iter.opaque
        inputs (%x: !mo.tensor<[M, N], f32>)
        outputs (%out: !mo.tensor<[M, 1], f32>) {
      map.iter.rowwise.body<[M, N], axis = 1>
          row (%row: !map.index<2>)
          capturing (%x0 = %x : !mo.tensor<[M, N], f32>,
                     %out0 = %out : !mo.tensor<[M, 1], f32>) {
        %acc = map.iter.reduce @builtin_kernels.monoids.ReduceSum
            index (%i: !map.index<2>) -> f32 {
          %v = map.load %x0[%i] : !mo.tensor<[M, N], f32>
          map.yield %v : f32
        }
        map.store %out0[%row] = %acc : !mo.tensor<[M, 1], f32>
      }
    }
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins MOSH_ShapeAttr:$shape,
                       I64Attr:$axis,
                       Variadic<AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>>:$captures);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.iter.reduce
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_IterReduceOp : MAP_Op<"iter.reduce", [
  ParentOneOf<["IterRowwiseOp", "IterRowwiseBodyOp"]>,
  SingleBlock,
  RecursiveMemoryEffects,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<OpAsmOpInterface, ["getAsmResultNames"]>,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<SymbolUserOpInterface>,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
]> {
  let summary = "A fold over the current row with a monoid";
  let description = [{
    Folds every element of the enclosing rowwise's current row with `monoid`,
    a `mogg.kernel.decl` with a `reduction`. The region runs once per element
    at index `%i` and yields the element's contribution. The results are the
    monoid's output fields, in order, one value per row, and print with the
    fields' names.

    The region reads the row and must not store.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %acc_values, %acc_indices = map.iter.reduce @builtin_kernels.monoids.ArgMax
        index (%i: !map.index<2>) -> (f32, si64) {
      %v = map.load %x[%i] : !mo.tensor<[M, N], f32>
      map.yield %v : f32
    }
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins FlatSymbolRefAttr:$monoid);
  let results = (outs Variadic<AnyType>:$results);
  let regions = (region SizedRegion<1>:$body);

  let hasCustomAssemblyFormat = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;

  let extraClassDeclaration = [{
    ::mlir::BlockArgument getIndexArg() {
      return getBody().front().getArgument(0);
    }
    YieldOp getYield();
  }];
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.constant.scalar
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_ConstantScalarOp : MAP_Op<"constant.scalar", [
  ConstantLike,
  Pure,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>,
]> {
  let summary = "A compile-time scalar constant, as a value not a tensor";
  let description = [{
    The single element of a compile-time constant, replacing the `map.load`
    that would read it (see `LoadOp`'s canonicalizer). The result has the
    loaded tensor's element type, so it is interchangeable with `map.load`.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %cst = map.constant.scalar 2.000000e+00 : f32 : f32
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins TypedAttrInterface:$value);
  let results = (outs AnyTypeOf<[AnyFloat, AnyInteger]>:$result);

  let assemblyFormat = "$value attr-dict `:` qualified(type($result))";
  // `ConstantLike` requires a folder for `m_Constant` to recover the value.
  let hasFolder = 1;
  let hasVerifier = 1;
}

//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//
// map.load
//===----------------------------------------------------------------------===//

def MAP_LoadOp : MAP_Op<"load", [
  TypesMatchWith<"result type matches tensor element type",
                 "tensor", "result",
                 "::M::MO::castFromTensorLike($_self).getElementType()">,
  TypesMatchWith<"index type matches tensor rank",
                 "tensor", "index",
                 "::M::MAP::IndexType::get($_self.getContext(), "
                 "::M::MO::castFromTensorLike($_self).getRank())">,
  Pure,
  DeclareOpInterfaceMethods<LowerableToMOGGInterface>
]> {
  let summary = "Load a value from a tensor at an N-D index";
  let description = [{
    Loads the element at an N-dimensional index from a tensor (or, fused into
    an in-place kernel, a buffer). Logically one scalar per index; the lowering
    may load a wider vector or tile.

    Example:
    ```mlir
    %xv = map.load %x[%idx] : !mo.tensor<[8, 16, 128], f32>
    ```
  }];

  let arguments = (ins AnyTypeOf<[MO_Tensor, MO_Buffer]>:$tensor, MAP_AnyIndex:$index);
  let results = (outs AnyType:$result);

  let assemblyFormat = [{ $tensor `[` $index `]` `:` qualified(type($tensor)) attr-dict }];
  let hasCanonicalizer = 1;
}

def MAP_StoreOp : MAP_Op<"store", [
  TypesMatchWith<"value type matches tensor/buffer element type",
